chunks: 34. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from Muhammad ibn Abu 'Umayr, from Abu Hamzah al-Thumali, from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both), who said:

Verily, Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, has assigned an angel to regulate prices, who manages them with His Command. And Abu Hamzah al-Thumali said: High prices were mentioned to Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both), so he said: 'I do not have authority over their high prices; if they rise, it is upon them (the angel/God), and if they lower, it is upon them.'

The Compiler of this book (may Allah be pleased with him) said: High prices (Ghala') is the increase in the prices of items to the extent that an item is sold for more than what it was sold for in that place, and low prices (Rukhsh) is the decrease in that. Whatever of low or high prices is due to the abundance or scarcity of items, that is from Allah, the Mighty and High, and it is obligatory to be pleased with that and submit to Him. And whatever of high or low prices is caused by what is taken from people for no lack of items or excess of them, without their approval, or is due to one person purchasing all the food of a town causing the food to become expensive for that reason, then that is from the Price-Fixer (al-Mus'ir) and the Transgressor, by purchasing all the food of the city, as Hakim ibn Hizam did. When food entered Medina, he would buy it all. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) passed by him and said: 'O Hakim ibn Hizam! Beware of hoarding.'

key_terms.الْمُسْعِر: The one who fixes prices artificially

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on price fixing and hoarding according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq contextualizes divine decree (al-Su'r) by distinguishing between natural fluctuations in supply and demand, which are attributed to Allah, and artificial manipulation like hoarding (ihtikar), which is a human transgression. The narration highlights the Prophet’s specific warning to Hakim ibn Hizam, establishing a foundational Shia legal principle for market regulation and consumer protection. This distinction underscores the balance between accepting divine providence in economic shifts and holding individuals accountable for unjust practices that harm the community.
